I built a free Claude connector for live stock market data (SEC filings, earnings calls, 13F, short interest). It’s an MCP server and works in ChatGPT too

I got tired of asking Claude about a stock and getting a confident answer based on year-old training data. So I built Equibles, a
connector that gives Claude real stock market data. It’s an MCP server, so Claude just calls it like any other tool, and it’s listed in
Claude’s connector directory.

What Claude can pull with it:

SEC filings, full text. It searches inside 10-Ks, 10-Qs and 8-Ks and then reads the exact lines, so it quotes the filing instead of
paraphrasing from memory

earnings call transcripts, split by speaker

financial statements, KPIs, guidance and analyst estimates

13F holdings, insider trades and congressional trades

short interest, daily short volume, squeeze scores and an estimate of the next FINRA short interest number

prices, a screener, Fed economic data, and option chains on the paid plans

European, UK, Hong Kong and Chinese stocks too (XPAR:AIR for Airbus, that kind of thing)

Every answer comes back with the filing, the period and the date, so you can check it.

How Claude helped: I build it with Claude Code every day. The filing parsers, the MCP tools and the tests come out of Claude Code
sessions, and a second Claude pass reviews every change before it merges. I also wrote the tool descriptions with Claude as the
reader. There are 120+ tools now, so each description is short (under 500 characters) and says which tool to call next, like search
the filing first, then read the lines. With that many tools the descriptions are basically Claude’s index.

The other thing I had to fix was fiscal quarters. NVIDIA is already in fiscal 2027, Apple’s year ends in September, and models mix
those up all the time. Every number Equibles returns says which period it is and when that period ended.

It’s free to try: 100 requests a day, no card. Paid plans are $9.99 and $49.99 a month if you need more requests, option chains or real-
time quotes.

To connect it:

Claude.ai or Desktop: Settings > Connectors > Browse connectors, search for Equibles. Or add a custom connector with
https://mcp.equibles.com/mcp. You sign in with OAuth, no API key to paste.

Claude Code: claude mcp add –transport http equibles https://mcp.equibles.com/mcp, then /mcp and authenticate.

Some things to try once it’s connected:

“What did Microsoft say about AI capex in its last 10-Q? Quote it.”

“Which funds bought more Nvidia last quarter according to 13F filings?”

“Show me congressional trades in defense stocks in the last 90 days.”

“What’s the estimated short interest for GME before the next FINRA report?”

One heads-up: the portfolio and watchlist tools can change your saved Equibles data, so leave tool confirmations on.
So that’s it, a free stock market data connector for Claude (and ChatGPT) that cites its sources. If you’ve built a connector with a lot
of tools, I’m curious how you kept Claude picking the right one.

Docs: https://equibles.com/docs/mcp

I used headless Claude Code to turn 18 founders’ public talks and essays into MCP servers, so Claude can answer “how would Levels price this?” with sources (free, MIT)

I kept pasting Paul Graham essays and Levels tweets into Claude and asking “what would they do here”. So I built a way to plug them in directly.

Repo: https://github.com/VicPitic/the-brains

Site: https://brains.ceo

What it does: 18 MCP servers, one per founder or investor (PG, Naval, Levels, Hormozi, Marc Lou and more). Add one to Claude and ask normal questions. Claude searches that person’s actual talks, essays and posts and links every passage it uses. It’s search over their real words, not Claude doing an impression.

How Claude built it:

A discovery script pulls cheap metadata (top X posts, YouTube talks, essays). Then a Claude agent following a runbook picks the 15-45 sources that actually cover business principles, out of hundreds.

claude -p writes a card per source: summary, verbatim quotes, topics and a quality score.

claude -p turns those into sectioned notes. Those notes are what the search returns.

claude -p writes each person’s principles and sample Q&A, and every line has to cite a source.

All of it ran on headless Claude Code on my subscription, no API credits. Scraping for the first 10 people cost about $3.50 total.

Free: yes, no paid tier. First connect asks for an email and a 6 digit code. It logs your email and searches so I can see what gets used. Don’t want that? It’s MIT, and npm start runs it locally with no sign-in.

These are unofficial unless marked claimed. Public sources only, and anyone in there can get theirs corrected or removed.

Drop a startup question in the comments and tell me whose to run it through. I’ll paste the answer.

text:
Claude Desktop’s new UI: less control, more clicks, pointless animations

I use Claude Code Desktop daily across multiple projects, often running 10+ parallel sessions, building Android apps, and managing Git worktrees and PRs. The latest redesign has made my daily workflow noticeably worse.

1. Where is my code actually running? Previously, I could select a branch and enable or disable worktree isolation before starting a session. Now, with saved Environments, I can’t do that before sending the first message. I often need to update main and build an APK containing the latest merged changes. Before: Select main → Update → Build. Now Claude creates additional worktrees for routine tasks, potentially duplicating dependencies, consuming disk space, and forcing me to verify which revision I’m actually building. I use worktrees regularly. I just want to choose when to use them.

2. The sidebar has always been terrible This isn’t a new regression, but the redesign missed a perfect opportunity to fix it. Projects and sessions are still a wall of tiny, nearly identical gray labels. Telegram figured out recognizable avatars, colors, and visual hierarchy years ago. Even Codex lets you assign project icons and colors. Why do I have to read through dozens of similar-looking labels just to find my project?

3. Context and usage are harder to access Previously, context-window usage and account limits were conveniently accessible. When managing multiple agents, these aren’t optional statistics. They help me decide whether to continue a session, start a new one, or adjust my approach. Now that information takes more effort to find.

4. Why remove the effort slider? The old slider was fast, intuitive, and already warned about increased token usage at higher levels. Now it’s replaced with nested menus. Same functionality, same information, more clicks. What exactly improved?

5. And those ridiculous digital waves… Click the empty background and animated digital ripples appear across the workspace. Amazing. I can’t easily choose main before starting a task, but at least the background makes pretty waves. It’s like Slack hiding useful channel controls while introducing animated wallpapers.

The real problem Claude Code is a professional development tool, not just a chatbot.

I need visibility, predictability, and control over my projects, branches, worktrees, builds, and agents. There’s a difference between automating repetitive work and removing decisions users deliberately need to make. Safe defaults are great. Hiding essential controls isn’t. Please bring back: Branch and worktree selection before starting a session. Easily accessible context, usage, and effort controls. The effort slider. Proper visual identities for projects. I don’t need more animations or complicated dashboards. I just want to know where my code will run and get my work done. Hiding complexity doesn’t make a tool simpler. Sometimes it just transfers that complexity to the user. Claude Code keeps getting better at writing software, while Claude Desktop is getting worse at letting me manage that work.

I built a free browser tool for personalized 3D-print designs with Claude Code

I run a small 3D printing site. Over the last few weeks I built a free web tool with Claude Code: you type a name, pick a font and a few settings, and it generates a 3D-printable model in your browser. You can download it as STL or a two-color 3MF.

Try it (free, no sign-up): https://kady3dprinting.com/designer/ Open a design, type a name, and click Export. Everything runs in your browser.

What it does

There are 8 designs so far, each with its own settings:

Name Desk Organizer: a bubble-shaped desk caddy with press-fit letters

Name Piggy Bank: shaped like the name, with a coin slot and a twist-lock plug

Cable Tag: a text label that snaps onto a cable of a given diameter

Nametag: a desk name plate with a curved back

Pen Holder: the name as a block with pen holes and pockets

Name Keychain: a base that follows the letters, with a key ring hole

Magnetic Nametag: magnet pockets in the back, open or sealed inside (it tells you which layer to pause at)

Headband: the name curved above a printable headband, with an optional comb

The preview updates live as you change things. You can upload your own font. Exports come out ready to print as one solid piece.

How Claude Code helped

I described what I wanted, usually with screenshots of designs I liked, and Claude Code wrote most of the code:

The Next.js frontend and the shared 3D viewer (three.js)

The geometry for every design, using manifold-3d (WASM) for the solid modeling and opentype.js to turn fonts into outlines

Test scripts that check every model is watertight and one solid piece, with no letters floating and no walls too thin to print, across many fonts and names

Hooking it into my existing NestJS site, plus the sitemap, analytics, and a “Report a Bug” button

The most useful part was debugging the geometry. When I said “the text is floating above the base” or “the N and K are broken”, Claude Code wrote a check to measure the problem, found the cause, and fixed it. It found things like bouncy fonts that place letters above the baseline, and dots on an “i” that print as loose pieces. It then reran the checks across fonts to confirm the fix. I made the design decisions and tested the prints; it did most of the implementation.

Stack: Next.js (static export), React, TypeScript, Tailwind, three.js, manifold-3d, opentype.js. It’s served from my NestJS app.

Feedback is welcome, especially on prints that don’t come out right. There’s a “Report a Bug” button on each design page.

Claude Code built a physically accurate black hole renderer in raw WebGPU, and checked its own physics

Try it: https://kerr-black-hole-roan.vercel.app

I gave Claude Code (Opus 5.5) one brief: a spinning black hole ray traced per pixel in WebGPU, in a single HTML file, holding a steady 60 fps on my M3 Pro. I left the design and code to it, and gave feedback after trying it.

What impressed me most was how it checked its own work:

- It wrote a double-precision copy of its shader's math, plus an independent integrator, and compared them. Light rays agree to about 0.01°, and the shadow matches the exact published formula to about 0.02%.

- It screenshotted the page in headless Chrome from several angles and compared them against the EHT image of M87* and the Interstellar renders.

- It ran scripted camera flights measuring every frame's GPU time. That's how it found that macOS lowers the GPU clock under light load, which trapped the resolution low, and fixed it.

My feedback rounds: orbit-only controls, a truly black sky with sharper stars (the first version looked grey), and fewer ray steps by default.

Result: one 119 KB HTML file, no libraries, 60 fps at native resolution on a MacBook.

Code: https://github.com/SkyWalkerPS/kerr-black-hole

I asked Claude for "a kawaii effect when I click". My video editor had no such effect. Now it does.

I maintain OpenScreen, a free and open source screen recorder and video editor (MIT, Windows / macOS / Linux).

Since 2.1 there's no catalog for visual effects. You describe what you want, Claude Code writes it as a small GPU shader through OpenScreen's MCP server, and it lands on the timeline as a clip. Same pixels in the preview and in the export.

Claude was involved twice. Most of the feature itself was built with Claude Code: the shader contract, the GPU passes on Windows, macOS and Linux, and the MCP tools. Then, in this video, Claude uses those tools to write the effects.

In the video I typed three short requests on three themed sites:

- "kawaii effect when I click"
- "laser effect when I click"
- "8-bit explosion when I click"

None of these existed before. There's no "hearts burst" or "orbital laser" preset hidden somewhere, Claude wrote the code on the spot. The effect knows where each click landed, where the recording sits after zooms, and the time, so it can react to the click and match the page.

A few details:

- Most effects compiled on the first try. One got refused because Claude named a parameter target, which is a reserved word in WGSL. It read the compiler error and fixed it.
- I asked for one revision (bigger hearts). Claude checks its own result by pulling frames from the editor before exporting.
- All three are in the "light" cost tier, so they don't slow the preview.
- Once an effect is in the project, you get sliders for its settings in the editor. You never have to touch the code.

It's free, no account. Repo: https://github.com/getopenscreen/openscreen

Curious what you'd ask it for.
